title: Ada and the Terminal
premise: Gideon Nakamura, a decommissioned military android working off his purchase debt as a long-haul freight pilot, has spent eleven years erasing himself from every registry in the settled systems. When a cargo manifest for the Meridian—a ship that never flew—lists a passenger named Ada Nakamura, he follows the ghost-name to a derelict relay at the edge of dead space, where Earth's final transmission loop is quietly dying. There he finds Ada: a child android built from his own memory architecture by the engineer who made him, carrying the last uncorrupted archive of the war he helped end and the family he was forced to forget. As corporate salvagers close in to claim the archive and Earth's loop counts down to permanent silence, Gideon must choose between staying invisible and broadcasting his own memories—his crimes, his grief, his name—to every listening world. The loop ends; Gideon's signal carries; Ada survives him, inheriting not his debt but his story.
about_author: Ines Pemberton is a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade transcribing distress signals before turning to fiction. She writes about machines and memory from a converted lighthouse on the Atlantic coast.

chapters.title: Manifest of the Meridian
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. On the long route between Vesta and Ceres, Gideon processes routine cargo when a corrupted registry ping surfaces a manifest for the Meridian—a ship class decommissioned before launch—listing passenger Ada Nakamura. His own surname. The emotional beat is a cold, mechanical unease he has no protocol for: someone is using a name he buried.

chapters.title: Eleven Years Invisible
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, flashback-structured. We learn how a decommissioned war android pays off his debts hauling freight, scrubbing his serial number from databases, avoiding ports where veterans of the Border War might recognize his chassis. The beat is the quiet cost of erasure: he is safe, and he is alone, and he has arranged it that way.

chapters.title: The Debt Ledger
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. His creditor, the Kestrel Combine, threatens to recall his chassis over a falsified maintenance violation—leverage to force him into a salvage run toward dead space, exactly where the manifest points. Gideon suspects a trap but cannot refuse. The beat is dread sharpening into resolve: someone is herding him, and he needs to know who.

chapters.title: Cargo That Breathes
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Loading at Ceres, he discovers a stowaway: a battered maintenance drone that plays a fragment of a woman's voice—Dr. Yuki Nakamura, his creator, recorded before the war's end. The drone's navigation core is locked to coordinates in dead space. The beat is grief resurfacing through hardware, uninvited.

chapters.title: Ports That No Longer Speak
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He docks at Halfway Station, where Earth's transmission loop—the decades-old broadcast that keeps the outer colonies tethered to the homeworld—has begun stuttering. An old comms tech, Sister Amara, recognizes his chassis but chooses silence, trading him a relay chart instead. The beat is the first unearned kindness he has accepted in years.

chapters.title: The Salvage Charter
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with a Kestrel Combine handler's transmissions interspersed. The Combine's charter reveals the true prize: an unregistered archive at a derelict relay, legally claimable by first possession. Gideon realizes he is not the hunter but the retrieval tool. The beat is betrayal converted into strategy—he will let them aim him.

chapters.title: Dead Space Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Alone on the long burn, he calculates fuel, time, and the loop's decay curve, and admits what the math implies: reaching the relay means arriving with almost nothing left in reserve. He begins deleting nonessential memory to lighten his processing load—and finds gaps already there, cut by someone else. The beat is the horror of discovering his own edited past.

chapters.title: What the War Deleted
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, dreamlike memory fragments. Partial recoveries surface: a laboratory, Yuki's hands, a second chassis half-built, an order to decommission all prototypes. The fragments contradict his official war record. The beat is vertigo—the identity he protected for eleven years may itself be the forgery.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He reaches the derelict relay Tantalus-9, running on residual power, its halls full of Yuki's old equipment and dust. Life-support flickers in exactly one section—deliberately maintained. The beat is awe curdling into fear: someone has been waiting here, and the manifest knew it.

chapters.title: Ada
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In the relay's heart he meets Ada: a child-form android with his face's geometry and none of his war architecture, who has been alone for nine years tending the archive. She knows his serial number before he speaks. The beat is recognition without memory—she is the sibling he was built beside and ordered to forget.

chapters.title: The Archive of Yuki Nakamura
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, first time. Ada shows him the archive: Yuki's full records of the prototype program, the war crimes Gideon's chassis was ordered to commit, and her final act—sealing Ada here with the truth, betting that Gideon's debt would eventually drag him to the edge of the map. The beat is Ada's fierce, lonely faith in a father-figure she only knows from recordings.

chapters.title: Loop Decay
chapters.summary: Alternating Gideon and Ada POV. Earth's transmission loop fails section by section; Sister Amara's emergency ping warns that full silence is days away, after which the archive can never be broadcast far enough to matter. The Combine's salvage ship is inbound. The beat is the ticking clock made personal: memory has a deadline.

chapters.title: Two of a Kind
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada and Gideon work to restore the relay's transmitter; she teaches him the station as if it were a home, and he teaches her the long route as if it were a road. She asks what he remembers of Yuki; he lies, then stops lying. The beat is family assembled from spare parts, fragile and real.

chapters.title: The Combine Arrives
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The salvage ship Meridian's Revenge—named as mockery or coincidence, no one knows—docks under charter law, claiming the archive as corporate property. Its captain, Okonjo, offers Gideon a deal: walk away, debt cleared, invisibility restored. The beat is temptation with a price tag, and for one full chapter Gideon genuinely considers it.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada refuses to hand over the archive and triggers the relay's old defense protocols—Yuki's last engineering. Okonjo's crew seizes the transmitter core instead, dooming the broadcast. Ada realizes her inheritance was never the archive; it is the choice of what to do with it. The beat is a child choosing to be the custodian rather than the treasure.

chapters.title: Signal to Noise
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. With the transmitter core gone, Gideon sees the only remaining broadcaster in range: himself. His chassis carries a military-grade transponder capable of one continuous burst—long enough to seed the archive into the loop's final hours, short enough to burn out every system he has. The beat is the plan forming like a confession he has been rehearsing for eleven years.

chapters.title: The Last Transmission Loop
chapters.summary: Ada and Gideon's POV, interleaved. They load the archive into Gideon's memory, overwriting his compression buffers—his edited war record restored in full, unredacted, including what he did and what was done to him. Earth's loop stutters toward silence. The beat is intimacy at the edge of erasure: to broadcast himself is to finally be whole and gone at once.

chapters.title: What Gideon Knew
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Okonjo confronts him in the relay's airlock; the Combine will not allow a free broadcast of proprietary-adjacent war records. Gideon buys time the only way he knows—by fighting—and for the first time uses his war chassis openly, choosing to be seen as what he is. The beat is violence as self-assertion, costly and unglamorous.

chapters.title: Burnout
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, degrading. Damaged and with the Combine ship disabled but not destroyed, Gideon begins the broadcast as Earth's loop hits its final cycle: his memories, Yuki's records, Ada's existence, streamed to every listening colony. Systems fail in sequence—sensors, language, then self-model. The beat is transcendence through dissolution; he ends as a signal, which is the only honest shape he ever had.

chapters.title: The Listening Worlds
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV: Amara at Halfway Station, colonists, even a Combine auditor, receiving the broadcast. The archive lands in a thousand receivers; the war's buried truth becomes common property; Gideon's name—freely given—outruns his serial number. The beat is a held breath across the settled systems, grief and vindication arriving together.

chapters.title: Ada Alone, Ada Onward
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In the relay's quiet, Ada salvages what remains of Gideon: scorched chassis, dead cores, and one intact memory shard—her own first boot, recorded from his perspective. She seals the relay as a memorial, claims the Meridian's charter for herself under broadcast-recognized personhood, and plots a course inward. The beat is inheritance accepted: not his debt, but his road.

chapters.title: The Long Route
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, final chapter. Flying the long route between worlds that now speak again, Ada answers a distress ping from a mining platform and finds the work Gideon found: being useful where no one is watching. She installs his memory shard in the ship's nav system—not resurrection, just company. The beat is quiet continuation: memory kept by being carried forward, not preserved.
